title: Entropy
lead: How much information a source really carries, and how to calculate it.
sections: The definition
Shannon entropy is H = −Σ p log₂ p. It is the average number of yes-or-no questions needed to identify the next symbol when you ask the best possible questions.
Reading the formula
A rare event is more surprising, with −log₂ p bits of surprise. Entropy is the expected surprise. A fair coin gives 1 bit. A coin that lands heads 90% of the time gives about 0.47 bits.
Conditional entropy

H(Y|X) measures what remains uncertain about Y once X is known. For language, knowing the previous letter removes a lot of uncertainty. Shannon estimated that printed English carries only about 1 to 1.5 bits per letter once long context is included.
Limits of estimates
Entropy calculated from a short text is biased low, because rare patterns are missing. Compare only like with like: the same length and the same alphabet size.
example: Calculating H for AAB
The probabilities are 2/3 and 1/3. H = −(2/3)log₂(2/3) − (1/3)log₂(1/3) ≈ 0.39 + 0.53 = 0.92 bits per symbol.
solve: Entropy identifies what kind of text you have. Ciphertext from a simple substitution has the same entropy as its plaintext, while strong encryption approaches the maximum. The app's Voynich study found conditional entropy far below any of six languages.

title: Huffman and Shannon-Fano coding
lead: Give common symbols short codes, and approach the entropy limit.
sections: Prefix codes
If no codeword begins another codeword, a stream of bits can be decoded without separators. Morse needed pauses because it is not a prefix code.
Shannon-Fano, top down
Sort symbols by frequency and split them into two groups of nearly equal weight. One group gets 0 and the other 1, and you recurse. It is simple, but not always optimal.
Huffman, bottom up

Repeatedly merge the two least frequent nodes. David Huffman proved in 1952 that this gives the shortest possible average length of any symbol-by-symbol prefix code, as a student solving a problem set from Robert Fano.
The limit
Shannon's source coding theorem says the average length cannot fall below the entropy. Huffman stays within 1 bit of it. Arithmetic coding gets closer by encoding a whole message as one number.
example: Six symbols
With frequencies A 45, B 13, C 12, D 16, E 9 and F 5, Huffman gives an average of 2.24 bits per symbol. A fixed code needs 3 bits. Run this in the simulation to compare Shannon-Fano.
solve: Compression removes redundancy, and redundancy is what codebreakers exploit, so compressing before encrypting makes a cipher harder to attack. Compressing after encryption achieves nothing, which makes compressibility a quick test of whether a text is already encrypted.

title: Randomness and how to test it
lead: Random-looking is not the same as random, and security depends on the difference.
sections: What randomness means

Statistically, each bit should be unpredictable and independent. Kolmogorov's idea is that a string is random if no program shorter than the string can produce it. That quantity cannot be computed in general, so we test instead.
Statistical tests

The monobit test counts ones. The runs test counts changes between 0 and 1. A serial test checks pairs. NIST publishes a larger suite based on these ideas. A test can only reject randomness and can never prove it.
True and pseudo-random
Hardware sources use physical noise. Pseudo-random generators stretch a short seed. A good statistical generator can still be cryptographically useless if its output reveals its state.
Real failures
Debian's 2008 OpenSSL bug left only about 32,767 possible process-based seeds, making many keys guessable. Reused or poor randomness also exposed Sony's PS3 signing key.
example: The monobit statistic
With 4,000 bits and 2,100 ones, the statistic is |2×2100 − 4000| ÷ √4000 ≈ 3.16. That is above 2.58, so it fails at the 1% level.
solve: The app's pigeon-message study uses these ideas: letters that look perfectly random imply a key that cannot be attacked statistically.

title: LFSRs and Berlekamp-Massey
lead: A hardware random generator, and the elegant algorithm that defeats it.
sections: Linear feedback shift registers
A register shifts along and feeds back the XOR of selected bits. With good taps, an n-bit register produces a sequence of length 2ⁿ − 1 that passes many statistical tests.
Why linearity is fatal
Each output is a linear combination of earlier ones. The Berlekamp-Massey algorithm finds the shortest LFSR that generates a sequence from only 2L bits, where L is the register length.
Consequences
Stream ciphers must therefore combine LFSRs non-linearly. A5/1, used in GSM phones, relied on irregular clocking and was still broken.
example: Predicting the future
A 9-bit LFSR has a period of up to 511 bits, but 18 output bits are enough to find its feedback rule and predict every later bit.
solve: Known plaintext gives keystream bits directly by XOR. Berlekamp-Massey then turns that into complete prediction of the rest of the message.

title: Monte Carlo methods
lead: Answer hard questions by drawing random samples.
sections: The idea
If you cannot calculate an average exactly, sample and average those. Stanislaw Ulam and John von Neumann developed the method at Los Alamos in the 1940s.
Accuracy
Error falls in proportion to 1/√n, so 100 times as many samples gives 10 times the accuracy, whatever the number of dimensions.
Significance by simulation
To judge a result, repeat the analysis on shuffled data and see how often chance does as well. That empirical p-value needs no formula.
example: Estimating π
Throw darts at a unit square. The fraction landing inside the quarter circle tends to π/4, so 4 × that fraction estimates π.
solve: This is how the app guards against false discoveries. Every mystery result is compared against scrambled copies, and the Rubaiyat lead's 0.25% figure is a Monte Carlo estimate.

title: Markov chain Monte Carlo
lead: Wander through a huge space so that time spent matches probability.
sections: The problem
Often we can compute how plausible a key is only up to a constant, and there are far too many keys to list them.
Metropolis-Hastings
Propose a change. Accept it with probability min(1, new ÷ old). Run for long enough, the visits follow the target distribution.
Gibbs sampling
Update one variable at a time from its distribution given all the others.
Tuning
Steps that are too small explore slowly. Steps that are too big are nearly always rejected. Watch the acceptance rate and how fast the trace mixes.
Annealing
Raising the probability to a growing power concentrates the chain on peaks. That is simulated annealing, which seeks one best answer instead of the whole distribution.
example: Breaking a cipher
Persi Diaconis described a prisoner's coded note broken by a Metropolis walk on substitution keys scored with letter pairs from War and Peace.
solve: The app's solvers are this method. Homophonic solving, Playfair attacks and the Zodiac benchmark all search keys by a Metropolis rule.

title: Message passing and belief propagation
lead: Local conversations that solve global problems.
sections: Factor graphs
Draw variables as circles and constraints as squares. A code's parity checks form such a graph, called a Tanner graph.
Sum-product

Each node tells each neighbour what it believes, excluding what that neighbour told it. On a graph without loops, this computes exact probabilities. On loopy graphs it is an approximation that often works very well.
Log-likelihood ratios
Beliefs are carried as log-odds, so a large positive value means a confident 0. Combining evidence is then simple addition at variable nodes.
Where it is used
Gallager's low-density parity-check codes, rediscovered in the 1990s, approach Shannon's capacity using message passing. They are used in Wi-Fi and 5G.
example: A Hamming code
Seven bits obey three parity checks. Flip a bit in the simulation, and watch the checks push back until the belief changes sign.
solve: Message passing suits problems with many local constraints, such as filling in a damaged ciphertext, combining evidence from OCR engines, and sudoku.

title: Hidden Markov models and Viterbi
lead: Recover a hidden sequence from noisy observations.
sections: The model
Hidden states follow a Markov chain, and each state emits an observation. Here the hidden states are true letters, and the observations are noisy letters.
Forward-backward
This is belief propagation on a chain. It gives each position's most probable letter given all the evidence.
Viterbi
Dynamic programming finds the single most probable whole sequence, at a cost linear in length. Andrew Viterbi introduced it in 1967 for decoding convolutional codes.
Learning the model
Baum-Welch re-estimates probabilities from unlabelled data. Kevin Knight and others used this kind of approach to decode ciphers.
example: Repairing a word
If the noisy text reads THX, the bigram H to E is far more likely than H to X, so the model can prefer THE when the channel is noisy.
solve: This is exactly what is needed for OCR errors in historical ciphers, and for the Le Figaro scans in particular. It is planned as a next step in the app's OCR pipeline.

title: Variational inference
lead: Replace an intractable distribution with a simple one you can optimise.
sections: The trade
Monte Carlo is usually exact in the limit but slow. Variational inference picks a simple family of distributions, and finds the member closest to the truth.
Mean field
Assume all variables are independent. Each variable's belief is repeatedly updated using the average of its neighbours.
The lower bound
Minimising the Kullback-Leibler divergence is equivalent to maximising the evidence lower bound, known as the ELBO.
The price
Mean field is fast and deterministic, but it tends to be overconfident because it ignores correlations.
example: Cleaning a noisy image
Each pixel wants to agree with its noisy reading and its neighbours. In the simulation, compare the mean-field result with Gibbs sampling on the same task.
solve: When exact search is hopeless, a soft assignment of symbols to letters can be optimised quickly and used to start a stricter search.

title: Shor's quantum algorithm
lead: Why a large quantum computer would break RSA and elliptic curves.
sections: From factoring to periods
Choose a random a. The function aˣ mod N is periodic with some period r. If r is even and a^(r/2) is not −1 mod N, then gcd(a^(r/2) ± 1, N) reveals a factor.
The quantum part

A register holds all values of x in superposition. Computing f(x) entangles it with the results, and measuring f leaves only x values one period apart. A quantum Fourier transform then concentrates probability on multiples of Q/r.
Back to classical
A measurement k gives k/Q close to s/r. Continued fractions recover r.
Cost

Peter Shor showed in 1994 that this takes polynomial time. A classical computer simulating it needs exponential memory, so this page can only handle tiny numbers. Real attacks on 2048-bit RSA need error-corrected machines far beyond those built so far.
example: Factoring 15 with a = 7
The powers cycle 7, 4, 13, 1, so r = 4. Then 7² mod 15 = 4, and gcd(4 − 1, 15) = 3 and gcd(4 + 1, 15) = 5.
solve: Shor's algorithm is why NIST standardised post-quantum algorithms in 2024. It does not threaten symmetric ciphers in the same way: Grover's algorithm gives only a square-root speedup.

title: Differential and linear cryptanalysis
lead: How modern block ciphers are attacked, and how they are designed to resist.
sections: Differences
Study pairs of inputs with a fixed XOR difference. Key XORs cancel, so the difference passes straight through key mixing and only the S-boxes matter.
The difference table
For an S-box, count how often each input difference gives each output difference. Large entries are weaknesses.
Key recovery
Guess the last round key, undo the final S-box, and count how many pairs show the expected difference. The right key stands out.
Linear cryptanalysis
Mitsuru Matsui's 1993 method finds linear relationships among input, output and key bits that hold with probability away from one half. It was used in the first experimental break of full DES.
Design
Biham and Shamir published differential attacks around 1990. DES's S-boxes were already strengthened against them, as Don Coppersmith later confirmed.
example: A strong S-box
The PRESENT S-box has no difference-table entry above 4 out of 16, apart from the trivial zero difference.
solve: The app's toy cipher attack recovers a round key from chosen plaintext, showing in miniature how real block ciphers are evaluated.

title: Pollard's rho and factoring
lead: A random walk that bites its own tail.
sections: The idea
Iterate x → x² + c mod n. Modulo a hidden factor p the sequence must eventually repeat, tracing a shape like the Greek letter ρ.
The birthday effect
A cycle appears after around √p steps, not p, by the birthday bound. Floyd's tortoise and hare detects it with almost no memory.
Beyond rho
Larger numbers need the quadratic sieve or the general number field sieve, which hold the current records.
example: Factoring 8051
Starting from x = 2, the walk finds the factor 97 in a few steps, where trial division needs dozens.
solve: This is why RSA moduli must be large and need two similarly sized primes. Pollard rho also solves small discrete logarithms.

title: A catalogue of classic attacks
lead: The main ways ciphers fail, with somewhere to try each one.
sections: Attack models

Ciphertext-only: the attacker has only intercepted messages. Known plaintext: some message and ciphertext pairs are known. Chosen plaintext: the attacker can have messages encrypted. Chosen ciphertext: the attacker can have messages decrypted.
example: Why models matter
A cipher can resist ciphertext-only attacks while falling immediately to known plaintext. The Hill cipher is a classic example.
solve: Identifying what the attacker has access to is the first step in any real analysis.
